sessions.title: CPU

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: ● Beginner: What is a CPU core vs a thread?

● Senior: How does context switching impact performance, and how would you diagnose excessive context switching on a production server? ● Architect: How do you approach CPU capacity planning across a virtualized enterprise fleet, considering licensing costs, vCPU oversubscription ratios, and workload types?
anchors: Think of the CPU as a chef in a kitchen: cache is the ingredients on the counter (fast to grab), RAM is the pantry (slower, has to walk there), storage is the grocery store (much slower still). Cores are multiple chefs working in parallel; hyper-threading is one chef juggling two dishes efficiently but not truly cooking two at once.

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: The motherboard is the kitchen itself in our ongoing kitchen analogy — the counters, the plumbing, the electrical wiring that lets the fridge (RAM), pantry (storage), and chef (CPU) actually work together in the same space. sessions.title: Power

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: Power is the electricity flowing into the kitchen itself — without it, the fridge (RAM), the stove (CPU), and the pantry lighting (storage access) simply don't function, no matter how well-designed the kitchen (motherboard) is. A UPS is like a generator-powered flashlight you grab the instant the lights flicker — enough to finish plating the current dish safely, not to cook a full dinner.
sessions.summary: Power supplies and power delivery: wattage, efficiency, transient spikes, and UPS sizing.

anchors: If the motherboard (Session 4) is the kitchen and power (Session 5) is the electricity, firmware is the kitchen's very first automatic safety check the moment the lights come on — verifying the stove ignites, the fridge compressor runs, the outlets are live — before the chef (the OS) is even allowed to walk in and start cooking.

anchors: If Sessions 1-6 built one fully functioning kitchen, virtualization is building walls to divide that single kitchen into several independent kitchens, each with its own stove, fridge, and pantry access — sharing the same building, plumbing, and electricity (the physical hardware), but each chef (guest OS) believes they have their own private kitchen entirely.
sessions.summary: Virtualisation concepts, hypervisors, Type 1 vs Type 2, and VM resource overhead.

sessions.title: Boot Process

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: ● Intermediate: What's the difference between a bootloader and a kernel, and why are they separate stages?

● Senior: A server shows a blank screen after a hardware upgrade — walk through how you'd identify which boot stage is failing. ● Architect: How would you design a zero-touch, automated OS deployment pipeline (PXE, answer files/cloud-init) for provisioning dozens of new servers consistently?
anchors: Think of the boot process as a relay race: the firmware (Session 6) runs the first leg and hands the baton to the bootloader, which runs a short leg and hands off to the kernel, which runs a longer leg and hands off to the init system/services, which finally hands the baton to you at the login screen. If the race stalls, you just need to find which runner still has the baton.
sessions.summary: The full cold-boot sequence from power-on to a login prompt, and where it can break.

sessions.title: Memory Management

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: Think of virtual memory as a hotel: every guest (process) gets their own room number (virtual address) that always looks the same to them, but the hotel (OS/MMU) can quietly change which physical room (RAM frame) that number maps to, or even move the guest's stuff to storage (swap) without the guest noticing.
Page fault = 'the OS's librarian had to actually go fetch the book' — minor fault: book was in the back room (RAM, just not on your desk); major fault: book was in the off-site archive (disk).
Copy-on-write = 'shared Google Doc in view-only mode until someone tries to edit — only then does it fork into their own copy.'

OOM Killer = 'the fire marshal at max capacity: forcibly picks and removes whoever is taking up the most space' when the building (RAM+swap) is truly full. 17. Connections — Ties to Every Prior Session
Session 1 (CPU): the MMU that performs page-table walks and enforces protection rings lives inside the CPU; memory management is impossible without it.
sessions.summary: Memory management: virtual memory, paging, swapping, and OOM behaviour.

sessions.title: Drivers

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: Think of a driver as a translator at a business meeting: the OS speaks one universal business language (generic I/O calls), the hardware speaks its own native dialect, and the driver sits between them translating both directions in real time.
Kernel-mode driver = 'employee with a master key to every door in the building' — powerful and fast, but if they make a mistake, the damage isn't contained to one room.
ISR/DPC split = 'a nurse doing rapid triage (ISR: stop the bleeding, flag it urgent) before handing off to the doctor for the actual treatment (DPC: do the real work) later.'

BYOVD attack = 'sneaking in with someone else's valid employee badge (a signed but flawed driver) instead of forging your own — security checks the badge is real, not whether the badge-holder should be trusted with that door.' 17. Connections — Ties to Every Prior Session
Session 1 (CPU): drivers rely on CPU privilege rings (Ring 0 execution) and the interrupt controller to receive and handle hardware events.
sessions.summary: Drivers: the kernel interface, the driver store, and why signed drivers matter.

sessions.title: Services

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: Think of a service manager as a building's night shift supervisor: it knows which systems (services) must be running unattended overnight, in what order to switch them on, what to do if one trips a breaker (crashes), and it keeps a logbook (Event Log/journald) of everything that happened.
'Running but not healthy' = a shop's lights are on and the door is unlocked, but the cash register is broken — open for business by outward appearance, unable to actually serve anyone.

Service dependency ordering = a restaurant kitchen: you cannot plate the dish (start the app service) before the oven has preheated (the database is ready) — skip that ordering and you get a 'started' plate that's actually raw.

Least-privilege service account = giving the night janitor a key that only opens the supply closet, not the vault — they can still do their job, but a stolen key doesn't hand over everything. 17. Connections — Ties to Every Prior Session
Session 1 (CPU): every service process is ultimately scheduled onto CPU time slices exactly like any other process.
sessions.summary: Services and init systems, and how they differ between Windows and Linux.

sessions.title: Logging OSLevel

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between the Windows Application, System, and Security event logs?
Why is Event ID 1102 significant, and what does it tell an investigator?
Why might expected security events simply not appear in a log at all, even though nothing was cleared?
anchors: Think of OS logging as a building's security camera system: if a camera (audit category) was never installed pointed at a particular door, no amount of investigating afterward will produce footage of who walked through it.
Event ID 1102 (Security log cleared) = the equivalent of an alarm that goes off specifically when someone tries to erase the security tapes — the act of hiding evidence becomes evidence itself.
Facility.severity in syslog = an envelope's return address (facility: which department sent it) plus its urgency stamp (severity: how important it is) — routing rules sort mail by both together.

Centralized log shipping = mailing a copy of every important document to a safety-deposit box the moment it's created, so a fire (or an intruder) in the local office can't destroy the only copy. 17. Connections — Ties to Every Prior Session

Session 1 (CPU) and Session 2 (Memory): hardware-level errors (ECC memory faults, CPU machine- check exceptions) are among the earliest and most critical categories the kernel ring buffer/dmesg captures.
sessions.summary: Operating-system level logging: Windows event logs, syslog and journald.

sessions.title: File Systems

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: Think of a file system as a library's card catalog plus its shelves: the catalog (metadata/inode/MFT) tells you exactly where a book lives and who's allowed to check it out, while the shelves (data blocks) hold the actual pages — losing the catalog doesn't destroy the books, but it makes them nearly impossible to find.

Journaling = a construction crew's work order posted before they start: if the crew is interrupted mid-job, the next shift reads the work order to know exactly what was in progress and finish or undo it cleanly, rather than guessing from a half-built wall.

Inode exhaustion = a parking garage that's run out of numbered parking spots even though there's technically open pavement — the constraint isn't physical room, it's the fixed count of assignable slots.

Copy-on-write = never erasing a whiteboard, only writing the new version on a fresh whiteboard and then pointing everyone to the new one — the old board still exists intact until someone deliberately wipes it (a snapshot you can always roll back to). 17. Connections — Ties to Every Prior Session
Session 1 (CPU) and Session 2 (Memory): file system metadata lookups and page-cache operations consume CPU cycles and RAM exactly as any other kernel workload does.
sessions.summary: File systems: NTFS, ext4, XFS and their journaling behaviour.

sessions.title: Permissions

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: POSIX rwx = three keyrings on one keychain: owner, group, everyone else — always in that fixed order, always only those three.
chmod numbers = read(4) + write(2) + execute(1), like a simple point system per class — 7 means you unlocked all three, 5 means you skipped write.
NTFS Deny beats Allow = a bouncer's "no" always overrules a promoter's "yes," no matter how many promoters vouched for you.
SUID = wearing someone else's badge for one task only, then handing it back the moment the task ends.
Least privilege = giving someone the one specific key they need for their job, not a master key "just in case."
sessions.summary: Permissions and ownership: ugo/rwx, ACLs, and diagnosing permission problems.

sessions.title: Users

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: User account = employee badge; it proves identity to the system but doesn't itself open any doors — permissions and groups are the doors.
UID/SID = the badge's embedded chip, not the printed name on the front — the system trusts the chip, not the name.
Disable before delete = take the badge away and deactivate it, but keep it in the drawer in case HR or legal needs to ask questions about it later.
Service account = a badge issued to a robot, not a person — it never sleeps, never quits, and needs its own separate security policy.
Account lockout = three wrong door-code attempts and the keypad locks itself for a while — a defense against someone guessing all night.
sessions.summary: Users: local accounts, password aging, and service accounts.

sessions.title: Groups

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between Domain Local, Global, and Universal group scope in AD, and when would you use each?
A user was just added to a group but still can't access the resource — what's your troubleshooting process?
Why can nested groups be a security risk even when each individual group's permissions look reasonable?
anchors: Group = lanyard color; the security desk checks the lanyard, not each individual badge, and doors are configured once per color, not once per person.
A-G-DL-P = Accounts wear a Global lanyard for their role, and that lanyard gets clipped onto a Domain Local keyring that actually opens the door — Permissions live on the keyring, not the lanyard.
Nested groups = Russian nesting dolls of access — opening the outer doll doesn't tell you everything hidden inside the smaller ones without actually checking each layer.
Distribution group vs. security group = a mailing list sign-up sheet versus a building keycard — one routes messages, the other opens doors, and confusing the two is a real risk.
Stale group membership = an old lanyard nobody collected when someone changed teams — still opens doors it shouldn't, silently, until someone actually checks.
sessions.summary: Groups, memberships, and the difference between primary and supplementary groups.

sessions.title: Package Management

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: Package manager = hardware store inventory system: tracked, versioned stock that won't let you take the last box of bolts three other projects still need.

Low-level vs. high-level tool = the delivery truck driver (dpkg/rpm, installs exactly what's handed to them) versus the store manager (apt/dnf, figures out everything else that needs to be ordered first).
Dependency hell = trying to fit two custom-order parts into the same slot, where satisfying one supplier's spec breaks the other's.
Package signing = a tamper-evident seal on a shipped box — if the seal's broken or missing, you don't trust what's inside, no matter how legitimate the label looks.
Version pinning = deliberately keeping one specific tool in the toolbox even after a newer model comes out, because you know exactly why the old one still fits the job.
sessions.summary: Package management: RPM and dnf, repositories, and what Flatpak changes in RHEL 10.

sessions.title: Networking Stack

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: A user says they have an IP address but can't reach anything outside their subnet. What OS-level setting would you check first, and why?
What's the difference between TCP and UDP at the OS stack level, and when would an application choose one over the other?
What is ARP, and why does a host need it even if it already knows the destination IP address?
How would you troubleshoot "this one application can't connect to the server" when other applications on the same machine connect fine?
What's the difference between a host's routing table and a router's routing table?
anchors: Postal system analogy: Socket = mailroom clerk, TCP/UDP = signed-receipt-or-not decision, IP = address on the envelope, NIC driver = delivery truck.
Bottom-up troubleshooting mnemonic: "Link, Local IP, Local Gateway, Remote IP, Name, Port" — walk the stack from the wire up to the application.
"ipconfig /all shows you the truth, ipconfig alone shows you the summary" — always use /all when actually troubleshooting.
sessions.summary: The networking stack: sockets, the port table, and which services listen by default.

sessions.title: OSIModel

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Can you name and briefly describe all seven layers of the OSI Model, in order?
What's the difference between a packet, a frame, and a segment, and which OSI layer does each belong to?
Where does a switch operate in the OSI Model? Where does a router operate? Where does a firewall operate?
If a user can ping a server but can't load a website hosted on it, which OSI layers have you already confirmed are working, and which layer would you check next?
Why do we still teach a 7-layer model when most real-world networks are actually built on the 4-layer TCP/IP model?
What OSI layer does encryption (TLS) operate at, and why does that matter for security architecture?
anchors: Top-down mnemonic: "All People Seem To Need Data Processing" (7→1: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical).
Bottom-up mnemonic: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away" (1→7).
PDU chain: Bits (1) → Frames (2) → Packets (3) → Segments (4) — memorize this order since it's a very common fill-in-the-blank interview question.
"Switches switch frames (Layer 2), routers route packets (Layer 3)" — a quick way to recall device-to- layer mapping.
sessions.summary: The OSI model, what each layer actually does, and where real devices sit.

sessions.title: TCPIPModel

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: How many layers does the TCP/IP model have, and how do they map onto the seven OSI layers?
Why does the industry use TCP/IP in practice instead of the full OSI protocol suite?
What's the difference between the Internet layer and the Transport layer, in terms of what each one is responsible for?
If a firewall rule blocks a connection, which TCP/IP layer(s) does that rule typically operate at, and what fields does it match on?
Explain the difference between checking IP-layer reachability (ping) and Transport-layer reachability (port test) — why might one succeed while the other fails?
anchors: "OSI has 7 seats, TCP/IP has 4 — and 3 of OSI's seats (App/Pres/Session) got merged into TCP/IP's one Application seat, while OSI's bottom 2 (Data Link/Physical) got merged into TCP/IP's one Network Access seat."
Four-layer order, top to bottom: Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access — "A Tiny Internet Network."
Layer-to-question mapping: Internet layer answers "can I reach the IP?"; Transport layer answers "can I reach the port?"; Application layer answers "does the service actually respond correctly?"
TCP/IP is the model of what's actually deployed; OSI is the model of how we talk about it.
sessions.summary: The TCP/IP model and how it maps onto OSI. Encapsulation and headers.

sessions.title: Ethernet

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is a MAC address, how is it structured, and how is it different from an IP address?
What does a switch do with the destination MAC address of an incoming frame?
What is CSMA/CD, and why don't modern switched networks need it?
How would you troubleshoot a workstation that intermittently loses connectivity, using only switch-side information?
What is MAC flooding, and how does a switch's default behavior make it possible?
anchors: "MAC address = the device's permanent name tag; IP address = the device's current mailing address" — MAC is hardware-local, IP is logical and routable.
Frame order mnemonic: Preamble, Destination MAC, Source MAC, EtherType, Payload, FCS — "Please Deliver Some Everyday Packages, Fast."
"Switches switch on MAC (Layer 2), routers route on IP (Layer 3)" — carried over directly from Session 25's device-to-layer mapping.
CRC/FCS errors climbing on a switch port = think cable/physical first, not software."
sessions.summary: Ethernet: frames, MAC addresses, switches and how a switch learns.

sessions.title: Switching

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
What happens when a switch receives a frame for a destination MAC it doesn't have in its table yet?
What is a broadcast domain, and why does a single switch (without VLANs) represent one big broadcast domain?
You notice a MAC address flapping between two switch ports in the MAC address table — what could cause this, and how would you investigate?
What's the difference between an access-layer switch and a core-layer switch in enterprise network design?
anchors: Three switch behaviors, in order: Learn (record source MAC), Flood (if destination unknown), Forward/Filter (if destination known) — "Learn, Flood, Forward."
"Hub = dumb repeater (Layer 1), Switch = smart local postman (Layer 2), Router = smart long-distance postman (Layer 3)."
CAM table = switch's memory of "who lives on which port" — built from source MACs, used to look up destination MACs.
A flapping MAC address in the table is almost always a loop or duplicate MAC — treat it as an immediate red flag.
sessions.summary: Switching: frame forwarding, VLANs, and the switchport lifecycle.

sessions.title: Routing

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between a switch and a router, in terms of what each one does with a packet/frame?
What is a default route, and when does a router use it?
What's the difference between a static route and a dynamic route? When would you use each?
How does traceroute work, and what does it rely on (hint: TTL) to identify each hop?
A user can reach some networks but not others — how would you use a routing table and traceroute together to diagnose it?
anchors: "Switches deliver within a neighborhood (MAC), routers deliver between cities (IP)."
"The envelope (Ethernet frame) gets thrown away and rewritten at every post office (router); the letter inside (IP packet) stays the same all the way to its destination."
Default route = 0.0.0.0/0 = "anything not matched by anything more specific."
TTL countdown = traceroute's whole trick: each hop that decrements TTL to 0 replies once, revealing the path one hop at a time.
sessions.summary: Routing: longest-prefix match, administrative distance, metric, next hop.

sessions.title: Subnetting

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: How many usable hosts are in a /27 subnet? Walk me through how you calculated it.
Given the network 172.16.0.0/22, what is the network address, broadcast address, and usable host range?
What's the difference between a subnet mask and CIDR notation, and how do you convert between them?
What is VLSM, and why is it preferred over fixed-size subnetting in real enterprise design?
Two hosts have the same IP network portion but different subnet masks — what problem can this cause, and how would you detect it?
How would you subnet a /24 network to support 5 subnets, each needing at least 20 hosts?
anchors: "2 to the power of host bits, minus 2" — usable hosts formula, always subtract 2 (network + broadcast addresses).
Block size shortcut: 256 minus the mask's value in the interesting octet = the size of each subnet (e.g., 256 − 192 = 64).
"Network address = all host bits 0. Broadcast address = all host bits 1. Everything else in between is usable."
Common CIDR-to-hosts table worth memorizing cold: /24 = 254, /25 = 126, /26 = 62, /27 = 30, /28 = 14, /29 = 6, /30 = 2.
sessions.summary: Subnetting that survives contact with a real network, including IPv4 exhaustion.

sessions.title: IPv4

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between a classful and classless (CIDR) IPv4 address, and why did the industry move to CIDR?
Given 192.168.10.0/26, how many usable host addresses are there, and what's the broadcast address?
anchors: Session 24 (Networking Stack, OS-level): the OS network stack is where IPv4 addresses are actually configured and where the routing decision (local vs. gateway) is made in software.
Session 25 (OSI Model) / Session 26 (TCP/IP Model): IPv4 is the concrete, real-world protocol that fills the Network layer (OSI L3) / Internet layer (TCP/IP model).

Session 27 (Ethernet) & Session 28 (Switching): IPv4 packets must be framed by Ethernet and switched at Layer 2 for any local delivery to happen — the Internal Workflow section above depends directly on this.
Session 29 (Routing): IPv4 is the addressing scheme that routing protocols and routing tables (Session 36) actually operate on — routing is meaningless without an addressing system to route toward.
sessions.summary: IPv4 addressing, subnet masks, private ranges, and special addresses.

sessions.title: IPv6

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Why was IPv6 created, and why can't NAT alone solve the underlying problem long-term?
Explain the difference between SLAAC and DHCPv6 — when would an enterprise choose one over the other?
What replaces ARP in IPv6, and how does it work at a high level?
Why doesn't the IPv6 header include a checksum field, and is that a security risk?
What's a link-local address, and why does every IPv6 interface get one automatically?
What's a rogue Router Advertisement attack, and how do you defend against it?
If a company runs dual-stack today, what's a realistic long-term migration path away from IPv4?
anchors: Session 31 (IPv4): directly precedes this session; IPv6 is best understood as a point-by-point contrast — 32-bit vs. 128-bit, ARP vs. NDP, broadcast vs. multicast, static config vs. SLAAC.
Session 27 (Ethernet) & Session 28 (Switching): IPv6 packets still require Layer 2 framing and switching for local delivery — same dependency structure as IPv4.
Session 29 (Routing) & upcoming Session 36 (Routing Protocols): modern routing protocols (OSPFv3, BGP) explicitly support IPv6 address families alongside IPv4.
Session 30 (Subnetting): the same conceptual network/host split applies, though IPv6 conventionally standardizes on /64 subnets rather than IPv4's variable sizing.
sessions.summary: IPv6: addressing, compression, and transition mechanisms.

sessions.title: VLAN

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between an access port and a trunk port?
Why can't two devices in different VLANs communicate without a router or Layer 3 switch?
What is VLAN hopping, and what configuration mistake typically makes it possible?
What's the native VLAN, and why do security best practices recommend changing it from the default?
Describe "router on a stick" — what problem does it solve and what's its main limitation?
Why might an enterprise avoid VTP (VLAN Trunking Protocol) despite the convenience it offers?
You've been told two switches, same VLAN, can't reach each other. What do you check first, second, third?
anchors: Anchor 1 Access port = one VLAN, for end devices. Trunk port = many VLANs, tagged, for switch-to-switch/router links.
Session 27 (Ethernet) & Session 28 (Switching): VLANs are a logical feature built directly on top of standard Ethernet switching behavior covered in these sessions.
Session 29 (Routing): the exact mechanism (router, or Layer 3 switch SVI) that allows inter- VLAN communication is the same routing logic introduced there.
Session 30 (Subnetting) & Sessions 31–32 (IPv4/IPv6): the near-universal one VLAN-to-one subnet convention ties VLAN design directly to the addressing plans built in these sessions.
sessions.summary: VLANs: why they exist, 802.1Q tagging, and trunking.

sessions.title: STP

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What problem does STP solve, and what happens on a switched network without it if a physical loop exists?
What are the four (or five, including Disabled) STP port states, and what happens in each?
What's the practical difference between classic 802.1D STP and RSTP (802.1w)?
What is PortFast, and why is it specifically recommended for end-device ports but not switch-to- switch links?
Explain BPDU Guard vs. Root Guard — what does each protect against?
Why might a large data center design deliberately avoid STP in favor of a Layer 3 leaf-spine architecture?
A network engineer tells you they lowered a switch's STP priority to 4096. Why would they do that, and what effect does it have?
anchors: Session 27 (Ethernet) & Session 28 (Switching): STP is a protocol specifically designed to govern and protect the Layer 2 switching behavior established in these sessions.

Session 33 (VLAN): modern STP variants (PVST+/Rapid-PVST+/MSTP) are explicitly VLAN- aware, calculating spanning tree instances per VLAN or per VLAN group rather than a single tree for the whole switch fleet.

Session 29 (Routing): STP's Layer 2 loop-prevention role is the direct analog to how IP routing uses TTL to prevent Layer 3 routing loops — same underlying problem (loops), solved at a different layer with a different mechanism.
sessions.summary: Spanning Tree Protocol: why loops are catastrophic, and the states that prevent them.

sessions.title: LACP

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between LACP active mode and passive mode, and what happens if both ends are set to passive?
anchors: Session 27 (Ethernet) — LACP operates strictly over Ethernet point-to-point full-duplex links.
Session 28 (Switching) — the LAG is treated as a single logical switch port for MAC learning and forwarding.
Session 33 (VLAN) — trunked VLANs ride across the aggregated bundle; member ports must share identical VLAN config.
Session 34 (STP) — the entire reason LACP exists instead of plain parallel links is to present STP with one logical port instead of a loop.
Session 16 (Drivers) — NIC teaming/bonding is implemented partly in the OS network driver stack.
sessions.summary: Link aggregation: LACP, bonding, and hashing rules that surprise people.

sessions.title: Routing Protocols

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the fundamental difference between a distance-vector and a link-state routing protocol?
anchors: Session 29 (Routing) — this session is the automated version of the manual routing-table concept already covered.
Session 30–32 (Subnetting/IPv4/IPv6) — routing protocols exist to advertise and select paths to exactly the prefixes designed in those sessions.
Session 35 (LACP) — port-channel interfaces can run any of these routing protocols directly once IP addressing is applied on top.
Session 34 (STP) — STP solves Layer 2 loops; these protocols solve the equivalent problem (loop prevention) at Layer 3, using very different mechanisms (link-state maps, DUAL, AS-Path).
sessions.summary: Dynamic routing protocols: distance vector vs link state, and when to use each.

sessions.title: NAT

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between NAT and PAT?
anchors: Session 30–32 (IPv4/Subnetting) — NAT exists specifically to bridge RFC 1918 private space and scarce public IPv4 space defined in those sessions.
Session 29 & 36 (Routing/Routing Protocols) — traffic must already be routed toward the NAT device before translation can happen; NAT does not replace routing.
sessions.summary: NAT and PAT: how translation breaks return traffic, and how it is undone.

sessions.title: ACL

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: "Standard ACL is short-sighted" — it can only see the source, so place it near the destination or it blocks too much too early.
"Extended ACL sees everything, so stop it at the door" — place it near the source to save bandwidth on traffic that was always going to be denied.
Wildcard mask = 255 minus the subnet mask, octet by octet — "invert to get permission bits."
"No match, no mercy" — the implicit deny any at the end of every ACL is silent but absolute.
Palo Alto Security Policy = "ACL that remembers the conversation" — stateful, so you don't write the return-trip rule yourself.
sessions.summary: Access control lists: standard vs extended, and why rule order decides everything.

sessions.title: DNS

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between a recursive resolver and an authoritative name server?
Why does DNS use UDP by default, and under what conditions does it fall back to TCP?
What does a low TTL trade off against a high TTL, and when would you deliberately lower one?
What's the difference between DNSSEC and DNS-over-HTTPS — what problem does each actually solve?

A user says a website 'isn't working.' What are the first two or three DNS-related checks you'd run before assuming the server itself is down? 7. Why can't you put a CNAME record at the zone apex (the root of a domain), and how do cloud providers work around that?
anchors: "Root knows the TLDs, TLDs know the domains, the domain's own server knows the truth" — the referral chain in one sentence.
"Recursive does the walking, iterative is each step of that walk" — resolver type vs. query type, not two competing protocols.
TTL is a dial between freshness and load — turn it down before a change, turn it back up once stable.
"Is it DNS?" — the first question in almost every outage, because DNS failure looks identical to the destination itself being down.
DNSSEC = signed, not secret. DoH/DoT = secret, not necessarily signed. Different problems, different fixes.
sessions.summary: DNS: records, resolvers, caching, and how name resolution fails.

sessions.title: DHCP

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Walk me through the DORA process — what is broadcast, what is unicast, and why?
What's the difference between the T1 and T2 timers, and what happens at each?
Why does DHCP need a relay agent, and what specifically breaks without one?
How would you detect and stop a rogue DHCP server on a switched network?
A device shows a 169.254.x.x address — what does that tell you, and what's your first troubleshooting step?
What's the difference between a DHCP exclusion and a DHCP reservation?
How does DHCP option 82 help with both security and centralized DHCP for multiple VLANs?
anchors: "DORA" — Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge, in that order, every fresh lease.
T1 at 50%, T2 at 87.5%, expiration at 100% — "try the one you know, then try anyone, then start over."
"No relay, no reach" — broadcasts die at the VLAN boundary; a helper address is the bridge across it.
169.254.x.x = APIPA = DORA never finished — the address the OS assigns itself when no server ever answered.
DHCP snooping trusts the uplink, not the request — untrusted ports can't source DHCPOFFER/DHCPACK, full stop.
sessions.summary: DHCP: the DORA exchange, scopes, options, reservations, and lease failure modes.

sessions.title: ARP

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Why does a host ARP for its default gateway instead of the actual destination IP when the destination is off-subnet?
How does ARP spoofing actually work, and what does Dynamic ARP Inspection do to prevent it?
anchors: "Ask everyone, only the owner answers" — ARP request is broadcast, ARP reply is unicast.
"Off-subnet? ARP the gateway, not the destination" — the single most-tested ARP concept on CCNA.
Gratuitous ARP = "I'm here" — used both to check for conflicts and to announce a failover takeover.
ARP has no ID check — anyone can claim any IP, which is exactly why spoofing works and DAI exists.
arp -a first, ping second — checking the local cache costs nothing and rules out an entire failure category instantly.
sessions.summary: ARP: building the L2-to-L3 map, and why a wrong ARP cache is so hard to see.

sessions.title: ICMP

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: IP protocol numbers: ICMPv4 = 1, ICMPv6 = 58 — think "1 for the original, 58 for its v6 successor."
Type 8 = Echo Request ("ask"), Type 0 = Echo Reply ("answer") — lower number replies to higher number, mirroring request/response order reversed.
Type 11 = Time Exceeded → traceroute's TTL trick.
Type 3 Code 4 = Fragmentation Needed → the single most operationally important ICMP message to never block, because it's PMTUD's lifeline.
ICMPv6 133–137 = Neighbor Discovery family — remember "133 starts the conversation" (Router Solicitation) up through Redirect at 137.
sessions.summary: ICMP: ping, traceroute, and what each reply type actually tells you.

sessions.title: TCP

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between flow control and congestion control in TCP?
Why does TIME_WAIT exist, and why shouldn't it simply be disabled to "fix" port exhaustion?
How does a SYN flood attack work, and how do SYN cookies mitigate it without breaking normal connections?
A client can ping a server but cannot establish a TCP connection on the application's port — what layers/components would you check, in order?
anchors: Three-way handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK — "I want to talk / okay, and I want to talk too / okay, let's go."
Four-way teardown: FIN → ACK → FIN → ACK — each side says goodbye independently, unlike the handshake's combined SYN-ACK step.
Flow control = receiver's rulebook ("how much I can hold"); Congestion control = sender's rulebook ("how much the network can hold") — two separate windows, two separate purposes.
Fast retransmit trigger = 3 duplicate ACKs — remember "three strikes, resend."
SYN cookies defend against SYN floods by not committing memory until the handshake actually completes — "don't pay until they show up."
sessions.summary: TCP: the three-way handshake, sequence numbers, and what a SYN flood is.

sessions.title: UDP

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: UDP header = 8 bytes; TCP header = 20+ bytes — "UDP travels light."

DNS and DHCP both default to UDP — the two protocols nearly everything else depends on run on the protocol with no guarantees, which is why their application-layer designs build in their own light retry logic.
No handshake, no teardown — a UDP datagram is a postcard, not a phone call: sent and forgotten, no confirmation built in.
Amplification attacks love UDP because there's no handshake to prove the sender actually asked for the (much larger) response — "no ID required, no return trip check."
RTP/VoIP prefers UDP because a late retransmitted audio frame is worse than a dropped one — "better silent than stale."
sessions.summary: UDP: connectionless, and why DNS and DHCP both depend on it.

sessions.title: VPN

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: Tunneling = the envelope; encryption = the lock on it — two separate jobs, often done together but conceptually distinct.
Site-to-site = always-on network-to-network; remote-access = on-demand user-to-network — remember "sites don't log in, users do."
Tunnel mode encrypts the whole original packet; transport mode only encrypts the payload — "tunnel hides the whole envelope, transport just seals the letter."
MTU shrinks inside a tunnel because of added encapsulation headers — expect PMTUD and MSS- clamping to matter more here than on a normal path.
SSTP rides on TCP 443 specifically to blend in with ordinary HTTPS traffic and get through restrictive firewalls — "hide in plain sight."
sessions.summary: VPN fundamentals: tunnels, encapsulation and the trust boundary.

sessions.title: IPSec

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is a Security Association, and why does a working IPSec tunnel require at least two of them?
What is the difference between IKE Phase 1 and Phase 2, and what does each one actually negotiate?
Why does NAT break plain ESP traffic, and how does NAT-T solve that problem?
A site-to-site tunnel shows as established on both ends, but no traffic passes — what would you check first, and why? 6. Why is IKEv2 generally preferred over IKEv1 in new deployments?
anchors: SAs are one-way — a tunnel needs (at least) two, one per direction, which is why "traffic goes one way but not the other" is such a classic IPSec symptom.
AH authenticates only; ESP encrypts (and can authenticate too) — "ESP does more, which is why it won."
Phase 1 = protect the negotiation itself; Phase 2 = negotiate protection for the actual traffic — "secure the phone line, then discuss the secret."
NAT-T wraps ESP in UDP 4500 specifically so NAT devices have ports to translate — "give NAT something familiar to work with."
IKE runs on UDP 500 (and 4500 with NAT-T) — remember "500 to start, 4500 once NAT gets involved."
sessions.summary: IPSec: transport vs tunnel mode, and the two phases that negotiate security.

sessions.title: SSL TLS

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography instead of just one or the other?
anchors: Asymmetric crypto sets up the conversation; symmetric crypto carries the conversation — "handshake with the slow, expensive key; talk with the fast, cheap one."
TLS 1.3 = fewer round trips, fewer legacy options — "faster and stricter, not just faster."
Forward secrecy (the "E" in ECDHE) means a stolen long-term key can't unlock yesterday's traffic — "fresh keys, no retroactive access."
Certificate chain = a chain of vouching, ending at a root the client already trusts — "trust travels down from a root you already believe."
SSL is dead; say TLS — but expect everyone, including this document's own conversational shorthand, to keep calling it "SSL" anyway.
sessions.summary: SSL/TLS: the handshake, certificate chain validation, and why padlocks are not proof.

sessions.title: Load Balancing

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

anchors: reads the letter."
TLS termination trades end-to-end encryption for routing visibility; passthrough trades routing visibility for end-to-end encryption — you can't fully have both at the same hop.
Cookie affinity follows the user; IP-hash affinity follows the network address — remember the NAT- gateway pitfall from this session's real example when choosing IP-hash.
A "healthy" backend per a shallow check ≠ a backend that can actually serve a real request — always ask what the health check actually verifies.
Least connections beats round robin specifically when connection duration varies — "round robin counts requests, least connections counts current work."
sessions.summary: Load balancing: algorithms, health checks, and where sessions stick.

sessions.title: Qo S

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is QoS and why does it only matter under congestion?
anchors: Simple mental hooks to make the concepts stick:
Classify → Mark → Queue/Schedule → Police/Shape: think of it as "sort the mail → stamp the envelope → decide the line order → decide who gets turned away or delayed."
DSCP = Layer 3, survives routing, more values (like a passport that works across countries). CoS =
EF (Expedited Forwarding) = voice's VIP pass — DSCP 46, always associate this specific number with voice priority.
Policing = bouncer (turns you away). Shaping = queue at the door (makes you wait, still lets you in).
sessions.summary: Quality of Service: classification, marking, queuing and shaping.

sessions.title: Wireless

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Why does a wireless network with 'full signal bars' sometimes perform badly?
anchors: Wireless = a shared room where everyone has to take turns talking (CSMA/CA), unlike wired Ethernet's private phone lines.
2.4 GHz = long range, few clean channels (1/6/11 only), crowded highway. 5/6 GHz = shorter range, many clean channels, open highway.
"Full bars" tells you volume, not traffic — signal strength ≠ available capacity.
WPA2/3-Personal = one shared house key for everyone. WPA2/3-Enterprise = individual key cards issued and revocable per person (802.1X/RADIUS).
Sticky client = a phone call you refuse to hang up even though you've walked into the next room and can barely hear anymore — 802.11k/v/r exist to make you hang up and redial sooner.
sessions.summary: Wireless: channels, interference, and how 802.11 differs from Ethernet.

sessions.title: Directory Services

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is a directory service, and how is it different from a general relational database?
anchors: Directory service = the organization's single phone book and org chart combined, that every other system looks up instead of keeping its own.
DIT = a tree, just like a filesystem — OUs are folders, entries are files, and a Distinguished Name is the full file path.
X.500 = the ambitious, heavyweight original blueprint. LDAP = the practical, TCP/IP-friendly version everyone actually built on.
Replication = photocopies of the phone book kept at every office, all kept in sync, so no single office losing power stops everyone else from looking someone up.
The directory is the root of trust — compromise it, and you've potentially compromised everything that trusts it, not just one system.
sessions.summary: Directory services: what a directory is, and why nearly everything binds to one.

sessions.title: Active Directory

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between a domain, a tree, and a forest in Active Directory?
anchors: AD = Session 51's generic directory concept, plus Kerberos, plus DNS integration, plus Group Policy, all bundled into one deeply interconnected Microsoft platform.
Domain Controller = a Windows Server holding a copy of NTDS.dit and answering "who is this, and what do they belong to" for its domain.

FSMO roles = the handful of jobs AD refuses to multi-master, because two DCs doing them simultaneously would cause chaos — think of them as five specific "single-signature-required" duties in an otherwise fully collaborative team.
Sites = AD's awareness of physical geography, so a laptop in the branch office doesn't waste 30 seconds authenticating across a WAN link to the head office.
SID, not name, is the real identity — renaming is safe, deleting-and-recreating is not.
sessions.summary: Active Directory: the forest, domain, DC and Global Catalog, and how a client finds them.

sessions.title: LDAP

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between LDAP and Active Directory?
anchors: DN reads like a mailing address, most specific first: 'cn (person), ou (department), dc (company)' — the reverse of how you'd write a street address, but the same idea of nesting.
389 is plain, 636 is a lock (6-3-6 — three extra digits, like a padlock combination, to remember it's the 'secured' one).
Bind = login. Search = look something up. Everything else (Add/Modify/Delete/ModifyDN) is 'the four ways to change the tree.'
'Search then bind' — the two-step pattern for username-based login: first find the DN, then authenticate as that DN.
sessions.summary: LDAP: the protocol under AD, bind types, and how to query it.

sessions.title: Kerberos

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Why does Windows prefer Kerberos over NTLM?
anchors: Three-headed dog, three parties: client, service, and the trusted KDC standing between them — the mythology maps directly onto the protocol's actual shape.
'TGT unlocks the ticket window; the service ticket unlocks the door.' Two different tickets, two different purposes — don't present a TGT directly to an application.
Port 88 for Kerberos — small number, first thing that happens at 'logon time.'
Clock skew breaks Kerberos before passwords ever do — when in doubt, check NTP first.
sessions.summary: Kerberos: tickets, the KDC, and why time skew breaks authentication.

sessions.title: NTLM

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the main structural difference between NTLM and Kerberos authentication?
anchors: Three messages: Negotiate → Challenge → Authenticate — 'N-C-A,' the opposite order of Kerberos' 'you prove yourself first' flow; here the server challenges you first.
'The hash IS the key' — unlike a password, if an attacker has the NT hash, they don't need to crack it to use it. That's the whole pass-the-hash problem in one line.
Member servers can't validate NTLM alone — they have to phone a Domain Controller (Netlogon) every time. Kerberos services validate locally. That's the structural cost of NTLM's design.
IP address instead of hostname = no SPN = no Kerberos = NTLM fallback, guaranteed.
sessions.summary: NTLM: the older protocol, its weaknesses, and how it still appears in mixed networks.

sessions.title: DNS Integration AD

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Why does Active Directory depend so heavily on DNS?
anchors: 'DC Locator runs before Kerberos, before LDAP, before anything else' — DNS is the very first hop in any domain logon, which is why it's the first thing worth checking, not the last.
SRV record = 'where's the service,' not 'what's the IP' — a fundamentally different question than an A record answers.
_msdcs = forest-wide, site-scoped SRV = site-local preference — two layers of the same discovery mechanism, one broad, one local.
'AD-integrated' means the DNS data lives inside AD's own database, replicated by AD itself — not a separate system that merely talks to AD.
sessions.summary: How AD DNS actually works: SRV records, the _msdcs zones, and why DNS breaks join first.

sessions.title: Trusts

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: If Domain A trusts Domain B, who can access what?
anchors: 'The trusting domain opens its door; the trusted domain's users are the ones who get to walk through it.' Trust direction = direction of access being granted, always.
Trust answers 'can I believe you,' permissions answer 'are you allowed in' — two separate questions, both required.
Transitive = 'flows downstream automatically' (A trusts B trusts C, so A trusts C); non-transitive = 'stops exactly where you drew the line.'
Referral tickets are Kerberos's way of saying 'I don't handle this realm, but I know someone who does' — the cross-realm equivalent of a phone transfer to the right department.
sessions.summary: Trusts: one-way, two-way, transitive, and the security cost of each.

sessions.title: Forests

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is Active Directory's actual security boundary — the domain or the forest?
anchors: 'Forest = the whole property, Domain = a building on it.' Different buildings can have different local rules (password policy), but the property line (schema, forest-wide trust, Enterprise Admins) is shared by everyone on the lot.
Global Catalog = 'the whole forest's yellow pages, abridged' — full detail for your own domain, quick-reference summary for everyone else's.
3268/3269 = Global Catalog ports, always paired mentally with 389/636 from Session 53 as 'the forest-wide version of the same idea.'
If it says 'Enterprise Admins' or 'Schema Admins,' think forest-wide, not domain-wide — a completely different blast radius than 'Domain Admins.'
sessions.summary: Forests, domains and the Global Catalog as the price of scale.

sessions.title: Domains

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Strong Answer What's the difference between a domain, a tree, and a forest?
anchors: Domain = the smallest security boundary with its own database partition, password policy, and admin group — think "the actual walls," where a forest is "the property line."
Three domain-only FSMO roles: RID (IDs), PDC Emulator (time + legacy + urgent changes), Infrastructure (cross-domain references) — remember as "IDs, Time, References."
Every domain login is DNS → Kerberos → Database: find the DC, prove who you are, look up what you're allowed to do.
Domain Admins group = keys to the kingdom; Tier 0 protection exists specifically because of this.
Entra ID is a cousin, not a clone — flat tenant, web protocols, synced from on-prem via Entra Connect in most real deployments.
sessions.summary: Domains, OUs, and structuring an object model that survives staff turnover.

sessions.title: Group Policy

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Strong Answer What order does Group Policy apply in, and which setting wins on conflict?
anchors: LSDOU — Local, Site, Domain, OU — the processing order, closest-to-object wins by default.
Enforced beats Block Inheritance — the one exception that flips normal precedence, and a favorite interview trap.
GPC in AD (metadata) + GPT in SYSVOL (actual files) — two storage locations, two replication paths, one common source of "it's inconsistent" bugs.
90 minutes + random offset = the default refresh cycle; gpupdate /force to skip the wait.
gpresult /h report.html — the one command that turns "why isn't this applying" from a guess into a five-minute answer.
sessions.summary: Group Policy: scopes, security filtering, and the order settings apply in.

sessions.title: PKI

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Strong Answer What's the difference between the public key and the private key, and which one is ever shared?
anchors: Public key shared, private key secret, signature proves possession of the private key without revealing it.
Root offline, intermediate online — protect the trust anchor by minimizing its exposure.
CRL = list you download; OCSP = question you ask live; stapling = the server asks so the client doesn't have to.
A certificate is a signed statement: "this public key belongs to this identity," nothing more.
Internal PKI needs its root pushed to trust stores (via Group Policy); public PKI is already trusted everywhere by default.
sessions.summary: PKI: what a certificate authority is for and how trust anchors work.

sessions.title: Certificates

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Strong Answer Why does a certificate with the correct Subject field sometimes still fail hostname validation?
anchors: SAN, not Subject CN, is what hostname validation actually checks today.
Key Usage = what the key can cryptographically do; EKU = what purpose it's allowed to serve — both can silently block an otherwise-valid certificate.
PEM is text, DER is binary, PKCS#12 (.pfx) bundles cert+key+chain together with a password.
Wildcard = convenience with concentrated blast radius; SAN/per-service certs = more management overhead, smaller blast radius.
openssl x509 -text -noout is the go-to command to actually read what's inside a certificate rather than guessing.
sessions.summary: Certificates: issuing, renewal, and the expiry outage nobody planned for.

sessions.title: Federation ADFS

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Strong Answer What problem does federation solve that a domain trust (Session 59) doesn't?
anchors: IdP issues and signs, SP trusts and consumes — the password never crosses that boundary.
SAML = XML, older, enterprise-classic; OIDC = JWT, newer, built on OAuth 2.0.
Golden SAML is Golden Ticket's federation-layer cousin — steal the signing key, forge trust for anyone, anywhere it's trusted.
Seamless SSO = the same Kerberos TGT from Session 59 doing double duty at the federation layer.
Claim Rules decide what gets asserted; a misconfigured rule is an over-privileging risk, not just a broken-login risk.
sessions.summary: Federation and ADFS: joining two identity worlds without duplicating passwords.

sessions.title: SSO

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between SAML and OIDC, and when would you choose one over the other?
anchors: SSO = one login, many doors — the IdP hands the user a signed 'note' the SP trusts instead of asking for a password itself.
SAML = XML wearing a suit to a 2005 enterprise meeting. OIDC = JSON built for phones and APIs.
The SP never touches the password — think 'bouncer checks the wristband, doesn't ask who put it on.'
Golden SAML = someone steals the stamp the bouncer uses to make wristbands, so they can make their own.
Kerberos SSO on the intranet = the ticket you got at the front gate this morning gets silently re- shown at every door inside — no new asking.
sessions.summary: Single sign-on: the promise, the trade-offs, and where it breaks.

sessions.title: MFA

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What makes something a valid 'second factor' — why doesn't a password plus a security question count as MFA?
anchors: MFA = know + have + are — mix categories, not copies. Two passwords is not MFA, it's just one factor said twice.
TOTP = a stopwatch both sides share — no network call needed because the code is 'time plus secret,' computed independently on both ends.
SMS MFA is a screen door — better than nothing, but SIM swapping walks right through it.
AiTM phishing beats TOTP/push because it just relays what you typed/approved in real time — but it can't relay a FIDO2 signature, because that signature is glued to the real website's address.
Push bombing = knocking until someone answers by accident — number-matching stops the 'accidental yes.'
sessions.summary: Multi-factor authentication: factors, fatigue attacks, and recovery paths.

sessions.title: Identity Governance

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the Joiner-Mover-Leaver model, and why is the 'Mover' event often the weakest link in practice?
Why does RBAC make access certification more tractable than reviewing individual permissions directly?
anchors: Governance answers 'should you still have this,' not 'are you who you say you are' — that's SSO/MFA's job.
Joiner-Mover-Leaver: grants pile up easily, but only a deliberate process takes them back down — like a closet that only gets cleaned on a schedule, not automatically.
RBAC = review the bundle, not every item — a manager certifies 'Finance Analyst,' not twenty separate permissions.
SoD = don't let one person write the check AND sign it — the classic fraud-prevention conflict rule.
Rubber-stamp certification is worse than no certification — it creates false assurance that something was checked when it wasn't.
sessions.summary: Identity governance: joiners, movers and leavers as a security control.

sessions.title: DNS Enterprise

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between AD-integrated DNS zones and traditional primary/secondary zone replication?
What is a dangling DNS record, and why does it create a subdomain takeover risk?
Why should zone transfers be restricted to specific IP addresses, and what mechanism authenticates a transfer?
anchors: DNS is the layer everything else silently trusts — when it breaks, the symptoms look like everything else's problem first.
Split-horizon = same question, different room, different answer — internal LAN vs internet gets a different IP for the same name.
A dangling CNAME is an unlocked door with your company's name still painted on it — decommission the resource, decommission the record, same pipeline.
AD-integrated DNS = many masters, one truth, replicated — no single primary bottleneck because AD's replication does the work.
DNSSEC signs, it doesn't hide — think 'tamper-evident seal,' not 'privacy envelope.'
sessions.summary: Enterprise DNS design: zones, delegation, forwarders and caching.

sessions.title: DHCP Enterprise Deployment

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: A user's laptop shows a 169.254.x.x address. What does that tell you, and what would you check first?
anchors: DORA = Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge — the same four steps from Session 40, now happening across scopes, relays, and redundant servers instead of one flat network.
T1 = 50% (quiet renewal), T2 = 87.5% (broadcast rebind), 100% = full restart from Discover — the '50 / 87.5 / 100' progression is the whole lease lifecycle in three numbers.
APIPA (169.254.x.x) on a screen = the device's own admission that DHCP completely failed — it's the network equivalent of a blank stare.
“Untrusted ports drop Offers” is the one-line summary of DHCP snooping.
sessions.summary: Deploying DHCP at enterprise scale: scopes, reservations, failover and relay.

sessions.title: NTP

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Why does Kerberos care about clock synchronization, and what's the default tolerance?
Why does NTP prefer slewing the clock over stepping it, and when would it step instead?
anchors: Stratum 0 = the atomic/GPS clock itself (not on the network); Stratum 1 = directly attached to it;
